pos: n. (the Gaelic kingdom straddling the North Channel, with lands in Antrim and in Argyll, which brought the Gaels and the Irish church into Scotland)
etymology: Irish Dál Riata, the portion or share of Riata, a legendary ancestor; dál is a division of a people.
biblical_def: Dalriada was a Gaelic kingdom with land on both sides of the North Channel, in north Antrim and in Argyll and the islands, which is why the Gaelic language and the Irish church came into Scotland at all. Its fortress was Dunadd in Kilmartin Glen, where a rock-cut footprint marks the inauguration place. In 574 Áedán mac Gabráin became king and Columba, who had come to Iona eleven years earlier, is said by Adomnán to have ordained him, which is the earliest recorded Christian inauguration of a king in these islands. Dalriada fought Bernicia, lost heavily to the Picts, and in the ninth century was united with Pictland under Cináed mac Ailpín to form the kingdom of Alba. The dictionary records Dalriada because its existence shows how little national borders govern the spread of the gospel: one people on two coasts of one sea carried a church from Ireland into Britain. Paul grounds both the division of nations and their boundaries in a single decree of God, and the worship promised in the Psalms is from all of them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a nation as a body of people under one government; a bound as a limit; a habitation as a place of dwelling; to glorify as to honor; and a kingdom as the dominion of a king.
webster_full: NATION, n. A body of people inhabiting the same country, or united under the same sovereign or government.
BOUND, n. A limit; the line which comprehends the whole of any given object or space; a boundary.
HABITATION, n. Act of inhabiting; state of dwelling; place of abode; a settled dwelling.
GLORIFY, v.t. To praise; to magnify and honor in worship; to ascribe honor to, in thought or words.
KINGDOM, n. The territory or country subject to a king; dominion; rule; sovereign power.
corruption_summary: Gaelic kingdom with lands in Antrim and Argyll, whose king Áedán was ordained by Columba, and which united with Pictland to form Alba.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that nations and their borders are God's arrangement and not an obstacle to his purpose. Paul tells the Athenians both halves at once: God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26). The worship he is gathering comes from every one of them: “All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord” (Psa 86:9).

The live temptation is to treat the church as the property of a people, which a kingdom like Dalriada immediately disproves, since one kingdom lay in two countries and its church belonged to neither. The end of the matter is announced over all of them together: “The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ” (Rev 11:15). And the certainty of that outcome rests on an oath about God's intention rather than any kingdom's strength: “as I have purposed, so shall it stand” (Isa 14:24).

pos: n. (the British kingdom of the Clyde valley, with its rock fortress at Dumbarton, which outlasted every other British realm in the north)
etymology: From Gaelic Srath Chluaidh, the valley of the Clyde; the earlier British name of its capital was Alt Clut, the rock of the Clyde.
biblical_def: Strathclyde was the British kingdom of the Clyde valley, with its fortress on the twin-peaked basalt rock at Dumbarton and its reach at times as far south as Cumbria. It was Christian from Roman times, and Kentigern, called Mungo, was its bishop at Glasgow in the sixth century; its people spoke a British tongue close to Welsh and kept their own church and dynasty for some six hundred years after the English conversion began. The Norse of Dublin stormed Dumbarton in 870 after a four-month siege and carried off the population; the kingdom revived, was drawn into the orbit of the Scots, and was finally absorbed into Scotland in the eleventh century. The dictionary records Strathclyde for the length of its endurance and for the limits of the rock that symbolised it. Scripture never makes the refuge a place. Moses calls the eternal God the refuge and the everlasting arms the support; the counsel of the LORD stands when every stronghold has fallen; and Christ's promise to his church is made against the gates of hell, not against the Norse.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a refuge as shelter from danger; counsel as deliberate advice and purpose; a church as the collective body of Christians; to prevail as to overcome; and remembrance as the keeping in mind.
webster_full: REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger.
COUNSEL, n. Advice; deliberation; consultation; purpose; design; the determination of the divine will.
CHURCH, n. A congregation of Christians; the collective body of Christians, or of those who profess to believe in Christ.
PREVAIL, v.i. To overcome; to gain the victory or superiority; to be in force; to have effect.
REMEMBRANCE, n. The retaining in mind of what had before been known; honorable memory; account preserved.
corruption_summary: British kingdom of the Clyde with its fortress at Dumbarton, Christian from Roman times, stormed by the Norse in 870 and absorbed into Scotland in the eleventh century.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that endurance is a gift held by persons and promises, not by strongholds. Moses hands a landless people a refuge that no siege can reach: “The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms” (Deu 33:27). The Psalmist sets the only plan that cannot be overturned against every scheme that can, “The counsel of the LORD standeth for ever” (Psa 33:11).

The live temptation at a place like Dumbarton Rock is to let the geography do the believing. Four months of siege took it in 870 and the British of the Clyde were carried off to the Irish slave market. What was promised to the church was a durability of another order, and it was promised against the worst adversary named in Scripture: “upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Mat 16:18). The individual share of that promise is stated plainly: “Surely he shall not be moved for ever: the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Psa 112:6).

pos: n. (the British kingdom of the north-west, probably centred on Carlisle, whose king Urien is the subject of the oldest Welsh praise poetry)
etymology: Welsh Rheged, of uncertain meaning; the name survives in Dunragit in Galloway.
biblical_def: Rheged was a British kingdom of the north-west, probably reaching from Carlisle and the Solway into Lancashire and perhaps across to Galloway, and almost everything known of it comes from poetry. Urien of Rheged and his son Owain are praised in verses attributed to Taliesin, which make Urien the chief British war leader against the Angles of Bernicia in the later sixth century; his court was at a place the poems call Llwyfenydd. Rheged was Christian, being part of the Romanised British north, and it disappeared into Northumbria early in the seventh century, probably by a dynastic marriage rather than a conquest. Its name is preserved in a single Galloway place name. The dictionary records Rheged for the problem of a church that has left almost no record. Scripture does not treat that as a reason to stop asking: it commands enquiry of the former age, it calls a people to ask for the old paths and walk in them, and it makes the telling of what God did in the fathers' days a duty to the children.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a path as a way beaten by feet; to enquire as to ask for information; to hide as to conceal; a generation as a succession of men; and old as having existed long.
webster_full: PATH, n. A way beaten or trodden by the feet of man or beast, or made hard by wheels; a course of life or conduct.
ENQUIRE, v.i. To ask a question; to seek for truth or information by asking questions; to search into.
HIDE, v.t. To conceal; to withhold or withdraw from sight or knowledge; to keep secret.
GENERATION, n. A single succession in natural descent; the people of the same period; progeny.
OLD, a. Advanced far in years or life; having existed long; of long continuance; ancient.
corruption_summary: British kingdom of the north-west, probably centred on Carlisle, whose king Urien is praised in the oldest Welsh poetry and which vanished into Northumbria.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church is commanded to look back and that the looking back is for walking, not for sentiment. Jeremiah gives the whole method and the usual response in one verse: “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls” (Jer 6:16). The duty passes down the line, “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4).

The live temptation with a kingdom known only from poems is either to invent a history for it or to dismiss it. Scripture is calm about the turnover of peoples, “One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh” (Ecc 1:4), and it also licenses honest research into what the former age actually did: “For enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers” (Job 8:8). Rheged's Christians left no chronicle, and the right response is to ask, not to fill the gap with guesses.

pos: n. (the primatial see of all England, founded by Augustine in 597, whose archbishop is the first bishop of the English church)
etymology: Old English Cantwaraburh, the stronghold of the men of Kent; the Roman name was Durovernum Cantiacorum.
biblical_def: Canterbury is the mother see of the English church. Augustine, sent by Gregory the Great, was given the old Roman town by Ethelbert in 597 and set his cathedral there rather than in London as Gregory had intended, so that the primacy of England has sat in a Kentish market town ever since. Theodore of Tarsus organised the whole English church from it in the seventh century, Anselm wrote the Proslogion and Cur Deus Homo as its archbishop, Becket was killed in its north transept in 1170 and the pilgrim traffic to his shrine paid for the rebuilding of the choir, Cranmer wrote the Prayer Book while holding the see and was burned at Oxford in 1556, and Laud was beheaded in 1645. The dictionary records Canterbury without granting what its office has often claimed. Scripture allows for one apostolic foundation and lists twelve names in the wall of the city, and it refuses to put any later see among them: the foundation is laid once, Jesus Christ, and the household is built upon the apostles and prophets with him as the corner stone.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a foundation as the basis of an edifice; an apostle as one sent forth by Christ to preach; a corner stone as the stone uniting two walls; a primate as the chief ecclesiastic; and a city as a corporate town.
webster_full: FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that part of a building which lies on the ground; the ground work of any thing.
APOSTLE, n. A person deputed to execute some important business; but appropriately, a disciple of Christ commissioned to preach the gospel.
CORNER STONE, n. The stone which lies at the corner of two walls, and unites them; the principal stone of a foundation.
PRIMATE, n. The chief ecclesiastic in the church; an archbishop who has jurisdiction over other bishops.
CITY, n. A large town; in a stricter sense, a corporate town; a town or collective body of citizens.
corruption_summary: Mother see of the English church, founded by Augustine in 597, held by Theodore, Anselm, Becket, Cranmer and Laud.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the apostolic foundation is closed and countable. John sees the wall of the city and the names in it: “the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb” (Rev 21:14). The city itself is identified by its architect and not by any see on earth, “a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10).

The live temptation at a primatial see is to make the chair itself a foundation, and the history of Canterbury is largely the history of that claim being pressed against York, against the Welsh church, against Rome and against the crown. Paul closes the question in two sentences that leave no vacancy. The household is “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20), and no one may add to the base: “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11). An archbishop is a servant of that structure, and Cranmer at the stake knew it.

pos: n. (the Kentish port at the narrowest crossing, with a Saxon church inside the Roman fort and a priory on the pilgrim road)
etymology: From British Dubras, the waters, the name of the stream; Roman Dubris, Old English Dofras.
biblical_def: Dover is the port at the narrowest part of the Channel, twenty-one miles from France, and it has been the door of England for two thousand years. Inside its Roman fort on the heights stands St Mary in Castro, a large Saxon church built against a Roman lighthouse that serves as its bell tower, one of the oldest buildings in the country still in use for worship. A house of canons was founded in the town and refounded as a Benedictine priory in 1131, and through it passed the pilgrims going to Becket's shrine and the scholars, exiles, legates and refugees going both ways. Huguenot and Walloon refugees landed there in the sixteenth century, and English exiles left from it under Mary. The dictionary records Dover for its traffic. It is a place that only ever made sense as a crossing, and Scripture describes the believer's whole position in that way: a stranger and a pilgrim whose city is not here, who is passing through a country he does not own, and who is therefore told what to abstain from while he travels.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a stranger as a foreigner; a pilgrim as a wanderer and traveller; to abstain as to forbear and refrain; continuing as lasting and permanent; and a shelter as that which protects.
webster_full: STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one who is not a citizen; a guest.
PILGRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveler; one that travels to a distance from his own country to visit a holy place.
ABSTAIN, v.i. To forbear or refrain from, voluntarily; particularly, to refrain from an indulgence of appetite.
CONTINUING, a. Lasting; enduring; permanent; abiding; remaining in the same state.
SHELTER, n. That which covers or defends from injury or annoyance; a protection; security.
corruption_summary: Kentish port at the narrowest crossing, with a Saxon church inside the Roman fort and a Benedictine priory on the pilgrim road.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the believer's standing in this world is that of a traveller, and Peter draws a moral conclusion from it rather than a romantic one: “I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul” (1Pe 2:11). The patriarchs held the same position knowingly, having “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13).

The live temptation at a port is to mistake movement for pilgrimage, and the Dover road carried a great deal of religious traffic that was going nowhere. The writer to the Hebrews states the fact that makes a Christian a traveller, which is not restlessness but a settlement elsewhere: “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). Meanwhile the shelter is not the harbour: “For thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy” (Psa 61:3), which was as true for the Huguenots landing as for the exiles leaving.

pos: n. (the Ouse town and county of Huntingdonshire, with an Augustinian priory, and the title borne by Selina Hastings, patroness of the evangelical revival)
etymology: Old English Huntandun, the huntsman's hill, from hunta, a hunter, and dun, a hill.
biblical_def: Huntingdon is a small town on the Great Ouse, the county town of the old county of Huntingdonshire, with an Augustinian priory founded in the twelfth century and dissolved in 1538. Oliver Cromwell was born there in 1599 and represented it in parliament. The name belongs to church history chiefly through the earldom: Selina Hastings, Countess of Huntingdon, widowed in 1746, spent nearly the whole of a great fortune on the evangelical revival, built or bought some sixty chapels, appointed Whitefield and other preachers as her chaplains, founded Trevecca College in Wales for training preachers, and in the end was forced by the Toleration Act proceedings of 1779 to register her chapels as dissenting, which created the Countess of Huntingdon's Connexion. The dictionary records Huntingdon for what she did with money. Scripture is specific about the uses of property in the hands of believers: goods are sold and parted as men have need, bread is dealt to the hungry, and the religion God calls pure is defined by the visiting of the fatherless and widows.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a possession as that which is owned; to part as to divide and distribute; need as want and necessity; to deal as to distribute; and pure as free from defilement.
webster_full: POSSESSION, n. The having, holding or detention of property in one's power or command; the thing possessed.
PART, v.t. To divide; to separate; to sever; to distribute among; to share.
NEED, n. Want; occasion for something; necessity; a state that requires supply or relief; poverty.
DEAL, v.t. To divide; to part; to separate; to distribute; to give in portions.
PURE, a. Separate from all heterogeneous matter; free from moral defilement; genuine; real; unmixed.
corruption_summary: Ouse town of the old county of Huntingdonshire, whose countess Selina Hastings spent a fortune on chapels, chaplains and Trevecca College for the revival.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that property in a believer's hands is for distribution. Luke reports the Jerusalem church doing it plainly: “And sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need” (Act 2:45). Isaiah had already specified what the fast God chooses actually consists of, “Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry” (Isa 58:7).

The live temptation for a wealthy patron is to treat the gospel as a cause to be sponsored rather than a word to be obeyed, and the Countess avoided it by the simple method of being present: she sat under the preaching she paid for and answered to the law when her chapels were challenged. Christ counts the plain acts as done to himself, “I was a stranger, and ye took me in” (Mat 25:35), and James fixes the definition that a chapel-building programme cannot replace: pure religion is “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27).

pos: n. (the Trent town of the East Midlands, in whose county the first English Baptists and the Pilgrim separatists were formed)
etymology: Old English Snotingaham, the homestead of Snot's people; the initial letter was dropped under Norman pronunciation.
biblical_def: Nottingham stands on the Trent on a sandstone ridge honeycombed with caves, a Danish borough and then an English county town. Its county produced an extraordinary share of English dissent. Thomas Cranmer was born at Aslockton in Nottinghamshire; Scrooby in the north of the county was the home of William Brewster and the meeting place of the separatist congregation that went to Leiden and then to Plymouth; Gainsborough across the Trent held the congregation of John Smyth and Thomas Helwys, and Helwys, a Nottinghamshire gentleman of Broxtowe Hall, returned from Amsterdam in 1612 to found the first Baptist church on English soil at Spitalfields and to write the first English plea for universal liberty of conscience, for which he died in Newgate. The dictionary records Nottingham for Helwys. He argued that the king has no authority over the soul, dedicated the book to James I, and paid for it with his life; Scripture is plain that the overcoming is by testimony and that those who overcome do not love their lives to the death.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a testimony as a solemn declaration; to overcome as to conquer; persecution as the infliction of pain for religion; to persecute as to pursue with harassing; and conscience as the moral sense.
webster_full: TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact; witness.
OVERCOME, v.t. To conquer; to vanquish; to subdue; to surmount; to get the better of.
PERSECUTION, n. The act or practice of persecuting; the infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed.
PERSECUTE, v.t. To pursue in a manner to injure, vex or afflict; to harass with unjust punishment or penalty for supposed offenses.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions.
corruption_summary: Trent county town whose shire produced Cranmer, the Scrooby separatists, and Thomas Helwys, author of the first English plea for liberty of conscience.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the means by which the church actually prevails against hostile power, which is testimony and endurance rather than leverage. John names both the ground and the cost: “And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11). Christ had put such men in a beatitude, “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10).

The live temptation is to expect that a reasonable argument reasonably made will be reasonably received, which is exactly what Helwys expected when he sent his book to the king with a civil inscription and was imprisoned for it. Paul states the normal case without softening it: “Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12). The great catalogue of faith ends with men the world did not recognise, “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38), and a Nottinghamshire gentleman who died in Newgate for a pamphlet belongs on that list.

pos: n. (the Severn town of the Welsh march, with a Benedictine abbey founded in 1083, long the chief seat of English government in Wales)
etymology: Old English Scrobbesbyrig, the fortified place of the scrubland; the Welsh is Yr Amwythig.
biblical_def: Shrewsbury sits in a loop of the Severn on the Welsh border, a Mercian burh and then the chief town of the march, from which English government in Wales was largely conducted. Roger de Montgomery founded a Benedictine abbey there in 1083; in 1137 the monks obtained the relics of the Welsh virgin Winefride from Gwytherin and carried them to Shrewsbury, which made the abbey a pilgrimage centre and is the one episode of its history most people have heard of. The town was the place where Welsh and English law met, where drovers sold, and where Charles I raised his standard's successor force in 1642. The dictionary records Shrewsbury for the border condition. To live on a march is to live where two jurisdictions grind, and the New Testament's instruction for Christians in that position is strikingly domestic: pray for kings so that a quiet and peaceable life may be possible, study to be quiet, mind your own business, work with your own hands, trust the LORD and do good. A frontier town is where that counsel costs something.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines quiet as still and peaceable; authority as legal power; business as employment and concern; to study as to apply the mind; and to trust as to confide in.
webster_full: QUIET, a. Still; being in a state of rest; not in motion; free from alarm or disturbance; peaceable.
AUTHORITY, n. Legal power, or a right to command or to act; the power exercised by a ruling body or person.
BUSINESS, n. Employment; that which occupies the time and attention; affair; concern; duty.
STUDY, v.i. To fix the mind closely upon a subject; to endeavor diligently; to muse; to be attentive.
TRUST, v.i. To confide; to rely; to depend with confidence on; to believe.
corruption_summary: Severn town of the Welsh march with a Benedictine abbey of 1083, which obtained the relics of Winefride in 1137 and became a pilgrimage centre.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how Christians are told to live under contested authority, and the apostolic instruction is unexpectedly ordinary. Prayer is to be offered “For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2), and the believer's own ambition is set low on purpose: “that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11).

The live temptation on a frontier is to make religion an instrument of the quarrel, and the abbey's acquisition of a Welsh saint's bones for an English town is a small and telling instance of it. The Psalter prescribes the opposite posture, action and dependence together: “Trust in the LORD, and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land” (Psa 37:3), with the modest blessing that follows honest work, “For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be” (Psa 128:2). Drovers and weavers in a march town could obey all of that without owning a relic.

pos: n. (the Nottinghamshire minster of the archbishops of York, a collegiate church made a cathedral in 1884)
etymology: Old English suth well, the south spring; the local pronunciation keeps the older form.
biblical_def: Southwell is a small town in Nottinghamshire whose minster was given to the archbishops of York in 956 and served for nine hundred years as a collegiate church of secular canons rather than a monastery, with the archbishop's palace beside it. Its Norman nave survives whole, with two western towers and a carved tympanum; its thirteenth-century chapter house holds the finest naturalistic leaf carving in England, oak, hawthorn, maple and vine cut from life by masons who evidently went out and looked. Byron is buried at nearby Hucknall and lived at Southwell as a boy. The college was dissolved and revived, and in 1884 the minster became the cathedral of a new diocese covering Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire. The dictionary records Southwell for the carved leaves. Nobody required them and nobody could see most of them well; they were done because the men who cut them loved the work and the house it was for. Scripture does not sneer at that affection: the Psalmist says he loves the habitation of God's house, and prefers a day in the courts to a thousand elsewhere.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a habitation as a place of dwelling; honour as esteem and dignity; a court as an enclosed space before a house; a doorkeeper as one who guards an entrance; and to contain as to hold within limits.
webster_full: HABITATION, n. Act of inhabiting; state of dwelling; place of abode; a settled dwelling; a mansion.
HONOR, n. The esteem due or paid to worth; high estimation; dignity; reverence; veneration.
COURT, n. A space enclosed, or a space before a house enclosed by a wall; an open area in a palace or temple.
DOORKEEPER, n. A porter; one who guards the entrance of a house or apartment.
CONTAIN, v.t. To hold, as a vessel; to comprehend; to comprise; to include; to restrain.
corruption_summary: Nottinghamshire minster of the archbishops of York, a collegiate church for nine hundred years, with England's finest naturalistic leaf carving; a cathedral since 1884.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that love for the place of worship is a scriptural affection and not a weakness. David states it without embarrassment: “LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth” (Psa 26:8), and the sons of Korah put the preference in numbers, “For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand” (Psa 84:10).

The live temptation runs in both directions, and Southwell has met both: a dissolved college whose canons had drawn revenues for generations, and a Victorian restoration that risked making the carvings the point. God himself attaches his name to a particular house, “For now have I chosen and sanctified this house, that my name may be there for ever” (2Ch 7:16); and the same king who built it asked the question that keeps the affection sober: “But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee” (1Ki 8:27). The masons cut leaves for a house whose tenant is not housed.

pos: n. (Waltham Abbey in Essex, Harold's foundation and burial place, where Cranmer in 1529 proposed consulting the universities on the king's marriage)
etymology: Old English weald ham, the homestead in the forest, from weald, woodland.
biblical_def: Waltham Abbey stands in the Essex forest north of London. Harold Godwinson refounded its church as a college of canons about 1060, was devoted to its Holy Cross, and by the oldest tradition was buried there after Hastings; Henry II refounded it as an Augustinian abbey in 1177 as part of his penance for Becket, and it became one of the richest houses in England, the last to be dissolved, in March 1540. Its chief moment is small and consequential. In the summer of 1529, with the court at Waltham to avoid plague, Thomas Cranmer was lodging in the house of a relative with two of his pupils when Gardiner and Foxe came to supper and the king's marriage came up; Cranmer suggested that the question be put to the universities as a matter of divinity rather than pursued at Rome as a matter of law. Foxe told the king, the king sent for Cranmer, and the English Reformation took the course it took. The dictionary records Waltham for that supper. A man's heart devises his way and the LORD directs his steps, and the counsel of the LORD stands for ever.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to devise as to contrive and plan; a step as a pace and a course of action; counsel as deliberate purpose; a heart as the seat of the will; and to accomplish as to complete and fulfil.
webster_full: DEVISE, v.t. To invent; to contrive; to form in the mind by new combinations; to plan; to scheme.
STEP, n. A pace; an advance or movement made by one removal of the foot; a gradation; a proceeding.
COUNSEL, n. Advice; deliberation; consultation; purpose; design; the determination of the divine will.
HEART, n. The seat of the affections and passions; the will; the seat of understanding and of purpose.
ACCOMPLISH, v.t. To complete; to finish entirely; to execute; to carry into effect; to fulfil or bring to pass.
corruption_summary: Essex abbey, Harold's foundation and burial place and the last house dissolved, where Cranmer in 1529 proposed putting the king's marriage to the universities.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence that works through conversations nobody planned. Solomon divides the labour between the man and his Maker in one line: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9). Cranmer devised a suggestion over supper; what came of it belonged to the counsel that “standeth for ever, the thoughts of his heart to all generations” (Psa 33:11).

The live temptation is to read such a turn either as a lucky accident or as a divine endorsement of everything that followed from it. Neither is available. God's government of a king is asserted without any claim that the king is good: “The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will” (Pro 21:1), and Henry VIII is a hard case for any other doctrine. What is guaranteed is the errand of God's word and not the character of its instruments: “it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it” (Isa 55:11).
